F. Güngör Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Faculty of Science and Letters, Affiliation: Istanbul Technical University, 80626, Istanbul, Turkey    V.I. Lahno Affiliation: Pedagogical Institute, 2 Ostrogradskogo Street, 36003 Poltava, Ukraine    R.Z. Zhdanov Affiliation: Institute of Mathematics, 3 Tereshchenkivska Street, 252004 Kyiv, Ukraine
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Group classification of a class of third-order nonlinear evolution equations generalizing KdV and mKdV equations is performed. It is shown that there are two equations admitting simple Lie algebras of dimension three. Next, we prove that there exist only four equations invariant with respect to Lie algebras having nontrivial Levi factors of dimension four and six. Our analysis shows that there are no equations invariant under algebras which are semi-direct sums of Levi factor and radical. Making use of these results we prove that there are three, nine, thirty-eight, fifty-two inequivalent KdV-type nonlinear evolution equations admitting one-, two-, three-, and four-dimensional solvable Lie algebras, respectively. Finally, we perform a complete group classification of the most general linear third-order evolution equation.

1 Introduction

The purpose of this article is classifying equations of the form

ut=ux​x​x+F⁡(x,t,u,ux,ux​x)u_{t}=u_{xxx}+F(x,t,u,u_{x},u_{xx}) (1.1)

which admit non-trivial Lie (point) symmetries. The standard Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation

ut=ux​x​x+u​uxu_{t}=u_{xxx}+uu_{x}

belongs to the family of evolution equations (1.1). Classification of the KdV equation with variable coefficients (vcKdV)

ut=f⁡(x,t)​u​ux+g⁡(x,t)​ux​x​xf⋅g≠0u_{t}=f(x,t)uu_{x}+g(x,t)u_{xxx}\qquad f\cdot g\neq 0 (1.2)

by their symmetries is done in Ref. [1], where it is shown that the vcKdV can admit at most four-dimensional Lie point symmetry group and those having four-dimensional symmetry group can be transformed into the ordinary KdV equation by local point transformations. In Ref. [2], Eq. (1.2) is investigated from the point of view of its integrability. It is shown, in particular, that equations of the form (1.2) with three-dimensional Lie point symmetry group have a property of ”partially integrability”.

Our motivation is the same as for classifying vcKdV equations. We start with a rather general class of nonlinear equations generalizing (1.2) for gx=0g_{x}=0. Note that any tt dependent coefficient of ux​x​xu_{xxx} in (1.1) can be normalized by a reparametrization of time. The main advantage of this classification is that, if we know the equation under study admits a nontrivial symmetry group, then it is usually possible to apply the whole spectrum of the methods and algorithms of Lie group analysis. This enables us to derive exact analytical solutions of equations under study, reveal their integrability properties, find linearizing transformations, etc. Note that the connection between Lie point symmetries and integrability was discussed in [2, 3].

Recently, a novel generic approach to group classification of low-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) has been developed in [4]. The full account of ideas and algorithms applied can be found in the review paper [5] where the approach in question has been applied to classify the most general second-order quasi-linear heat-conductivity equations admitting non-trivial Lie point symmetries. Here we adopt the same approach which basically consists of three steps. We first construct the equivalence group, namely the most general group of point transformations that transform any equation of the form (1.1) to a (possibly different) equation belonging to the same class. Also, we find the most general element of the symmetry group together with a determining equation for FF. As a second step, we realize low-dimensional Lie algebras by vector fields of the above form up to equivalence transformations. To this end, we use various results on the structure of abstract Lie algebras [6, 7, 8, 9]. A review of the classification results of non-isomorphic finite-dimensional Lie algebras can be found in [5]. In the last step, after transforming symmetry generators to canonical forms, we proceed to classifying equations that admit nontrivial symmetries. We do this by inserting these generators into the symmetry condition and solving for FF.

Let us mention that similar ideas have been used by Winternitz and coworkers for group classification of several nonlinear partial differential equations [1, 10, 11] and of discrete dynamical systems [12, 13, 14]. Note also that group classification of the nonlinear wave and Schrödinger equations in the same spirit has been done in [15, 16].

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we present the determining equations for the symmetries and the equivalence group. Section 3 is devoted to the classification of the equations invariant under low-dimensional symmetry groups. In Section 4 we perform a classification of linear equations in the class (1.1). A discussion of results and some conclusions are presented in the final Section.

2 Determining Equations and Equivalence Transformations

Lie algebra of the symmetry group of equation (1.1) is realized by vector fields of the form

X=τ(x,t,u)∂t+ξ(x,t,u)∂x+ϕ(x,t,u)∂u.X=\tau(x,t,u)\partial_{t}+\xi(x,t,u)\partial_{x}+\phi(x,t,u)\partial_{u}. (2.1)

In order to implement the symmetry algorithm we need to calculate the third order prolongation of the field vector field (2.1) [17, 18, 19]

pr(3)X=X+ϕt∂ut+ϕx∂ux+ϕx​x∂ux​x+ϕx​x​x∂ux​x​x{\rm pr^{(3)}}X=X+\phi^{t}\partial_{u_{t}}+\phi^{x}\partial_{u_{x}}+\phi^{xx}\partial_{u_{xx}}+\phi^{xxx}\partial_{u_{xxx}} (2.2)

where

ϕt=Dt​ϕ−ut​Dt​τ−ux​Dt​ξ,ϕx=Dx​ϕ−ut​Dx​τ−ux​Dx​ξ,ϕx​x=Dx​ϕx−ux​t​Dx​τ−ux​x​Dx​ξ,ϕx​x​x=Dx​ϕx​x−ux​x​t​Dx​τ−ux​x​x​Dx​ξ.\begin{gathered}\phi^{t}=D_{t}\phi-u_{t}D_{t}\tau-u_{x}D_{t}\xi,\hfill\\ \phi^{x}=D_{x}\phi-u_{t}D_{x}\tau-u_{x}D_{x}\xi,\hfill\\ \phi^{xx}=D_{x}\phi^{x}-u_{xt}D_{x}\tau-u_{xx}D_{x}\xi,\hfill\\ \phi^{xxx}=D_{x}\phi^{xx}-u_{xxt}D_{x}\tau-u_{xxx}D_{x}\xi.\hfill\\ \end{gathered}

Here DxD_{x} and DtD_{t} denote the total space and time derivatives. In order to find the coefficients of vector field we require that the prolonged vector field (2.2) annihilate equation (1.1) on its solution manifold

pr(3)​X​(Δ)|Δ=0=0,Δ=ut−ux​x​x−F.{\rm pr^{(3)}}X(\Delta)\Bigl|_{\Delta=0}=0,\quad\Delta=u_{t}-u_{xxx}-F. (2.3)

Equating coefficients of linearly independent terms of invariance criterion (2.3) to zero yields an overdetermined system of linear PDEs (called determining equations). Solving this system we obtain the following assertion.

Proposition 2.1.

The symmetry group of the nonlinear equation (1.1) for an arbitrary (fixed) function FF is generated by the vector field

X=τ(t)∂t+(τ˙3x+ρ(t))∂x+ϕ(x,t,u)∂u,X=\tau(t)\partial_{t}+(\frac{{\dot{\tau}}}{3}x+\rho(t))\partial_{x}+\phi(x,t,u)\partial_{u}, (2.4)

where the functions τ⁡(t)\tau(t), ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) and ϕ⁡(x,t,u)\phi(x,t,u) satisfy the determining equation

−3​ux​ρ˙−x​ux​τ¨−9​ux​ux​x​ϕu​u−3​ux3​ϕu​u​u+3​ϕt−9​ux​x​ϕx​u−9​ux2​ϕx​u​u−9​ux​ϕx​x​u−3​ϕx​x​x+3​(ϕu−τ˙)​F+(2​ux​x​τ˙−3​ux​x​ϕu−3​ux2​ϕu​u−6​ux​ϕx​u−3​ϕx​x)​Fux​x+(ux​τ˙−3​ux​ϕu−3​ϕx)​Fux−3​ϕ​Fu−3​τ​Ft−(3​ρ+x​τ˙)​Fx=0.\begin{array}[]{ll}&-3\,u_{x}\,\dot{\rho}-x\,u_{x}\,\ddot{\tau}-9\,u_{x}\,u_{xx}\,\phi_{uu}-3\,{u_{x}}^{3}\,\phi_{uuu}\\ &+3\,\phi_{t}-9\,u_{xx}\,\phi_{xu}-9\,{u_{x}}^{2}\,\phi_{xuu}-9\,u_{x}\,\phi_{xxu}-3\,\phi_{xxx}+3\left(\phi_{u}-\dot{\tau}\right)\,F\\ &+\left(2\,u_{xx}\,\dot{\tau}-3\,u_{xx}\,\phi_{u}-3\,{u_{x}}^{2}\,\phi_{uu}-6\,u_{x}\,\phi_{xu}-3\,\phi_{xx}\right)\,F_{u_{xx}}\\ &+\left(u_{x}\,\dot{\tau}-3\,u_{x}\,\phi_{u}-3\,\phi_{x}\right)\,F_{u_{x}}-3\,\phi\,F_{u}-3\,\tau\,F_{t}-(3\,\rho\,+x\,\dot{\tau})\,F_{x}=0.\end{array} (2.5)

Here the dot over a symbol stands for time derivative.

If there are no restrictions on FF, then (2.5) should be satisfied identically, which is possible only when the symmetry group is a trivial group of identity transformations. Here we shall be concerned with the identification of all specific forms of FF for which non-trivial symmetry groups occur. The basic idea is to utilize the fact that for an arbitrarily fixed function FF all admissible vector fields form a Lie algebra. This immediately implies the idea of using the classical results on classification of low-dimensional Lie algebras obtained mostly in late sixties [6, 7, 8]. Saying it another way, we need to construct a kind of representation theory on low-dimensional Lie algebras generated by Lie vector fields preserving the manifold (2.5).

Our classification is up to equivalence under a group of locally invertible point transformations

t~=T⁡(x,t,u),x~=Y⁡(x,t,u),u~=U⁡(x,t,u),\tilde{t}=T(x,t,u),\quad\tilde{x}=Y(x,t,u),\quad\tilde{u}=U(x,t,u), (2.6)

that preserve the form of the equation (1.1), but (possibly) change function FF into a new one, namely we have

u~t~=u~x~​x~​x~+F~​(x~,t~,u~,u~x~,u~x~​x~)\tilde{u}_{\tilde{t}}=\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}\tilde{x}\tilde{x}}+\tilde{F}(\tilde{x},\tilde{t},\tilde{u},\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}},\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}\tilde{x}}) (2.7)

Inserting (2.6) into (1.1) and requiring that the form of the equation be preserved, we arrive at the following assertion.

Proposition 2.2.

The maximal equivalence group ℰ\cal{E} has the form

t~=T⁡(t),x~=T˙1/3​x+Y⁡(t),u~=U⁡(x,t,u),\tilde{t}=T(t),\quad\tilde{x}=\dot{T}^{1/3}x+Y(t),\quad\tilde{u}=U(x,t,u), (2.8)

where T˙≠0\dot{T}\neq 0, Uu≠0U_{u}\neq 0.

We note that the Lie infinitesimal technique can also be used to obtain the equivalence group (2.8). It is straightforward to prove that the both approaches produce the same results.

We make use of equivalence transformations (2.8) to transform vector field XX into a convenient (canonical) form.

Proposition 2.3.

Vector field (2.4) is equivalent within a point transformation of the form (2.6) to one of the following vector fields:

X=∂t,X=∂x,X=∂u.X=\partial_{t},\quad X=\partial_{x},\quad X=\partial_{u}. (2.9)

Proof. Transformation (2.8) transform vector field (2.4) into

X→X~=τ(t)T˙(t)∂t~+[13(τT˙−1T¨+τ˙)(x~−Y)+τY˙+ρT˙1/3]∂x~+[τUt+(13τ˙x+ρ)Ux+ϕUu]∂u~.\begin{split}X\to\tilde{X}&=\tau(t)\dot{T}(t)\partial_{\tilde{t}}+[\frac{1}{3}(\tau\dot{T}^{-1}\ddot{T}+\dot{\tau})(\tilde{x}-Y)+\tau\dot{Y}+\rho\dot{T}^{1/3}]\partial_{\tilde{x}}\\ &+[\tau U_{t}+(\frac{1}{3}\dot{\tau}x+\rho)U_{x}+\phi U_{u}]\partial_{\tilde{u}}.\end{split} (2.10)

There are two cases to consider:

I.) ϕ=0\phi=0. Choose U=U⁡(u)U=U(u) so that we have

X~=τ(t)T˙(t)∂t~+[13(τT˙−1T¨+τ˙)(x~−Y)+τY˙+ρT˙1/3]∂x~+ϕUu∂u~.\tilde{X}=\tau(t)\dot{T}(t)\partial_{\tilde{t}}+[\frac{1}{3}(\tau\dot{T}^{-1}\ddot{T}+\dot{\tau})(\tilde{x}-Y)+\tau\dot{Y}+\rho\dot{T}^{1/3}]\partial_{\tilde{x}}\\ +\phi U_{u}\partial_{\tilde{u}}. (2.11)

Now if τ=0,\tau=0, then ρ≠0\rho\neq 0 (otherwise XX would be zero) we choose T⁡(t)T(t) to satisfy

T˙=ρ−3.\dot{T}=\rho^{-3}.

In this case X~\tilde{X} is transformed into ∂x~\partial_{\tilde{x}}.

If τ≠0\tau\neq 0, then we choose TT and YY to satisfy

T˙=τ−1,τ​Y˙+ρ​T˙1/3=0.\dot{T}=\tau^{-1},\quad\tau\dot{Y}+\rho\dot{T}^{1/3}=0.

With this choice of TT and YY vector field X~\tilde{X} is transformed into ∂t~\partial_{\tilde{t}}.

II.) ϕ≠0\phi\neq 0. If τ=ρ=0\tau=\rho=0 then we can choose UU to satisfy ϕ​Uu=1\phi U_{u}=1 so that we have X~=∂u~\tilde{X}=\partial_{\tilde{u}}. Otherwise, UU can be chosen to satisfy

τ​Ut+(13​τ˙​x+ρ)​Ux+ϕ​Uu=0.\tau U_{t}+(\frac{1}{3}\dot{\tau}x+\rho)U_{x}+\phi U_{u}=0.

Hence we recover Case I.

Summing up, the vector field (2.4) is equivalent, up to equivalence under ℰ\cal{E}, to one of the three standard vector fields ∂x,∂t,∂u\partial_{x},\partial_{t},\partial_{u}. This completes the proof.

f1​Fx3=1,\displaystyle f_{1}F^{3}_{x}=1,
Gt=f1​Gx​x​x+f2​Gx​x+f3​Gx+f4​G+f5,\displaystyle G_{t}=f_{1}G_{xxx}+f_{2}G_{xx}+f_{3}G_{x}+f_{4}G+f_{5},

and thus normalize f1​(x,t)→1f_{1}(x,t)\to 1, and set f2​(x,t)→0f_{2}(x,t)\to 0, f5​(x,t)→0.f_{5}(x,t)\to 0.

ut=ux​x​x+A⁡(x,t)​ux+B⁡(x,t)​u.u_{t}=u_{xxx}+A(x,t)u_{x}+B(x,t)u. (3.3)

So the equation ut=ux​x​xu_{t}=u_{xxx} has the highest symmetry within the class of equations (3.3). Its maximal finite-dimensional symmetry algebra is four-dimensional.

Note that according to [5] the class of nonlinear equations of the form

ut=F⁡(t,x,u,ux)​ux​x+G⁡(t,x,u,ux),F≠0,u_{t}=F(t,x,u,u_{x})u_{xx}+G(t,x,u,u_{x}),\quad F\not=0, (3.11)

contains five nonlinear equations admitting five dimensional symmetry algebras. Furthermore, an equation admitting six-dimensional symmetry algebra is equivalent to the heat equation. It is the linear heat conductivity equation ut=ux​xu_{t}=u_{xx} that possess the largest symmetry group within the class of second-order equations (3.11).

This is not the case for the class of third-order PDEs under consideration in the present paper. We shall see that there are examples of nonlinear equations that admits higher symmetry algebras than the linear equation does. For instance, the nonlinear Schwarzian KdV equation (4.14) admits a six-dimensional symmetry algebra.

In order to describe equations (1.1) that admit Lie algebras isomorphic to the Lie algebras having nontrivial Levi decomposition we need, first of all, to describe equations whose invariance algebras are semi-simple.

The lowest order classical semi-simple Lie algebras are three-dimensional. The next admissible dimension for classical semi-simple Lie algebras is six. Summing up, we conclude that the algebra sl(2,ℝ)⊕{∂u}\Sl(2,\mathbb{R})\oplus\{\partial_{u}\} is the maximal invariance algebra admitted by equation (4.8). It cannot be extended by specifying the form of an arbitrary function G~​(σ),σ=x2​ux​x−2​x​ux\tilde{G}({\sigma}),\ \ {\sigma}=x^{2}u_{xx}-2xu_{x}.

What remains to be done, is classifying equations (4.7), whose invariance algebras are isomorphic to semi-direct sums of semi-simple Levi factor and radical, i.e., whose invariance algebras have the following structure: sl⁡(2,ℝ)⊂+L.\Sl(2,\mathbb{R})\subset\hskip-10.81204pt+L. To perform this classification we utilize the classification of these type of Lie algebras obtained by Turkowski [21].

We choose sl⁡(2,ℝ)={v1,v2,v3}\Sl(2,\mathbb{R})=\{{\rm v}_{1},{\rm v}_{2},{\rm v}_{3}\} with

v1=−2t∂t−23x∂x,v2=∂t,v3=−t2∂t−23tx∂x−x3∂u.{\rm v}_{1}=-2t\partial_{t}-\frac{2}{3}x\partial_{x},\ \ \ {\rm v}_{2}=\partial_{t},\ \ {\rm v}_{3}=-t^{2}\partial_{t}-\frac{2}{3}tx\partial_{x}-x^{3}\partial_{u}.

According to [21], there is only one five-dimensional Lie algebra of the desired form sl⁡(2,ℝ)⊂+L\Sl(2,\mathbb{R})\subset\hskip-10.81204pt+L with L={e1,e2}L=\{e_{1},e_{2}\}, operators e1,e2e_{1},e_{2} satisfying the commutation relations:

[e1,e2]=0,[v1,e1]=e1,[v1,e2]=−e2,\displaystyle[e_{1},e_{2}]=0,\ \ [{\rm v}_{1},e_{1}]=e_{1},\ \ \ [{\rm v}_{1},e_{2}]=-e_{2},
[v2,e1]=0,[v2,e2]=e1,\displaystyle[{\rm v}_{2},e_{1}]=0,\ \ [{\rm v}_{2},e_{2}]=e_{1},
[v3,e1]=e2,[v3,e2]=0.\displaystyle[{\rm v}_{3},e_{1}]=e_{2},\ \ \ \ [{\rm v}_{3},e_{2}]=0.

as operators e1,e2e_{1},e_{2} are necessarily of the form (2.4), we easily get that

e1=|x|−3/2∂u,e2=t|x|−3/2∂u.e_{1}=|x|^{-3/2}\partial_{u},\quad e_{2}=t|x|^{-3/2}\partial_{u}.

However, checking the invariance criterion for the above realization we find that the algebra in question cannot be invariance algebra of an equation of the form (4.7).

According to [21], there exist three six-dimensional Lie algebras that are semi-direct sums of semi-simple Levi factor and radical, algebra LL being of the form L={e1,e2,e3}L=\{e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}\}. Non-zero commutation relations for e1,e2,e3e_{1},e_{2},e_{3} read as

OPEN1)\displaystyle 1) [v1,e1]=2​e1,[v2,e2]=2​e1,[v3,e1]=e2,\displaystyle[{\rm v}_{1},e_{1}]=2e_{1},\ \ [{\rm v}_{2},e_{2}]=2e_{1},\ \ [{\rm v}_{3},e_{1}]=e_{2},
[v1,e3]=−2​e3,[v2,e3]=e2,[v3,e2]=2​e3;\displaystyle[{\rm v}_{1},e_{3}]=-2e_{3},\ \ [{\rm v}_{2},e_{3}]=e_{2},\ \ [{\rm v}_{3},e_{2}]=2e_{3};
OPEN2)\displaystyle 2) [v1,e1]=e1,[v2,e2]=e1,[v3,e1]=e2,\displaystyle[{\rm v}_{1},e_{1}]=e_{1},\ \ [{\rm v}_{2},e_{2}]=e_{1},\ \ [{\rm v}_{3},e_{1}]=e_{2},
[v1,e2]=−e2,[e1,e2]=e3;\displaystyle[{\rm v}_{1},e_{2}]=-e_{2},\ \ [e_{1},e_{2}]=e_{3};
OPEN3)\displaystyle 3) [v1,e1]=e1,[v2,e2]=e1,[v3,e1]=e2,\displaystyle[{\rm v}_{1},e_{1}]=e_{1},\ \ [{\rm v}_{2},e_{2}]=e_{1},\ \ [{\rm v}_{3},e_{1}]=e_{2},
[v1,e2]=−e2,[e1,e3]=e1,[e2,e3]=e2.\displaystyle[{\rm v}_{1},e_{2}]=-e_{2},\ \ [e_{1},e_{3}]=e_{1},\ \ [e_{2},e_{3}]=e_{2}.

Solving the above relations we see that the corresponding realizations cannot be invariance algebras of equation (4.7).

Next, we consider seven-dimensional algebras from the Turkowski’s classification. According to [21] there are five inequivalent algebras of the targeted dimension. Four of them contain the above five and six-dimensional algebras as subalgebras. So we need to consider only the fifth algebra sl⁡(2,ℝ)⊂+L,\Sl(2,\mathbb{R})\subset\hskip-10.81204pt+L, where L={e1,e2,e3,e4}L=\{e_{1},e_{2},e_{3},e_{4}\} and the following commutation relations hold

[v1,e1]=3​e1,[v2,e2]=3​e1,\displaystyle[{\rm v}_{1},e_{1}]=3e_{1},\hskip 14.22636pt[{\rm v}_{2},e_{2}]=3e_{1},
[v3,e1]=e2,[v1,e2]=e2,\displaystyle[{\rm v}_{3},e_{1}]=e_{2},\qquad[{\rm v}_{1},e_{2}]=e_{2},
[v2,e3]=2​e2,[v3,e2]=2​e3,\displaystyle[{\rm v}_{2},e_{3}]=2e_{2},\hskip 14.22636pt[{\rm v}_{3},e_{2}]=2e_{3},
[v1,e3]=−e3,[v2,e4]=e3,\displaystyle[{\rm v}_{1},e_{3}]=-e_{3},\hskip 14.22636pt[{\rm v}_{2},e_{4}]=e_{3},
[v3,e3]=3​e4,[v1,e4]=−3​e4.\displaystyle[{\rm v}_{3},e_{3}]=3e_{4},\hskip 14.22636pt[{\rm v}_{1},e_{4}]=-3e_{4}.

The most general form of operators e1,e2,e3,e4e_{1},e_{2},e_{3},e_{4} satisfying the above relations is as follows:

e1\displaystyle e_{1} =\displaystyle= |x|−92∂u,e2=3t|x|−92∂u,\displaystyle|x|^{-\frac{9}{2}}\partial_{u},\hskip 28.45274pte_{2}=3t|x|^{-\frac{9}{2}}\partial_{u},
e3\displaystyle e_{3} =\displaystyle= 3t2|x|−92∂u,e4=t3|x|−92∂u.\displaystyle 3t^{2}|x|^{-\frac{9}{2}}\partial_{u},\hskip 14.22636pte_{4}=t^{3}|x|^{-\frac{9}{2}}\partial_{u}.

However, verifying the invariance criterion yields that this algebra cannot be symmetry algebra of equation (4.7).

Thus we proved that the class of PDEs (4.7) contains no equations admitting symmetry algebras of the dimension n≤7n\leq 7, which are semi-direct sums of Levi factor and radical. It is natural to conjecture that the same assertion holds for an arbitrary nn. To prove this fact we need to consider in full details classification of nonlinear equations (1.1), whose invariance algebras are solvable.

Let us sum up the above results as theorems.

Theorem 4.2.

The class of PDEs (1.1) contains two inequivalent equations whose invariance algebra are semi-simple (sl⁡(2,ℝ)\Sl(2,\mathbb{R}))

ut\displaystyle u_{t} =\displaystyle= ux​x​x−32​ux−1​ux​x2+ux​G​(x,t);\displaystyle u_{xxx}-\frac{3}{2}u^{-1}_{x}u^{2}_{xx}+u_{x}G(x,t);

ω1=3​u−x​ux,ω2=6​u−x2​ux​x.\displaystyle\omega_{1}=3u-xu_{x},\ \ \omega_{2}=6u-x^{2}u_{xx}.

The maximal invariance algebras of the above equations under arbitrary GG read as

Theorem 4.3.

Nonlinear equation (1.1) whose invariance algebra is isomorphic to a Lie algebra having non-trivial Levi decomposition is represented by one of the following equations:

ut=ux​x​x−32ux−1ux​x2+uxG~(x),sl1(2,R)⊕{∂t};\displaystyle u_{t}=u_{xxx}-\frac{3}{2}u^{-1}_{x}u^{2}_{xx}+u_{x}{\tilde{G}}(x),\quad\Sl^{1}(2,R)\oplus\{\partial_{t}\}; (4.10)

where G~\tilde{G} is an arbitrary function of xx or σ\sigma. Moreover, the associated symmetry algebras are maximal.

Note that equation (4.12) can be expressed in the form

utux={u;x},\frac{u_{t}}{u_{x}}=\{u;x\}, (4.14)

where {u;x}\{u;x\} denotes the Schwarzian derivative of uu with respect to xx. It is known that a non-point transformation taking this equation into the usual KdV exists.

5 Classification of equations invariant under low-dimensional solvable symmetry algebras

In this section we apply the strategy summarized in the Introduction to identify representative classes of equations of the form (1.1) invariant under one-, two-, and three-dimensional solvable symmetry algebras. In order to approach this task in a systematic manner we realize all possible inequivalent algebras in terms of vector fields (2.4) under the action of the equivalence group ℰ\cal{E}.

5.1 Equations with one-dimensional symmetry algebras

We assume that for a given FF, equation (1.1) is invariant under a one-parameter symmetry group, generated by the vector field (2.4) with coefficients subject to the constraint (2.5). We make use of Proposition 2.3 which characterizes the canonical forms of the vector field XX of (2.4). We then substitute the coefficients of the canonical vector field into the determining equation (2.5), which is a first order linear homogeneous PDE for FF, and solve the latter in order to construct invariant equations.

According to Proposition 2.3 we have three types of one-dimensional symmetry algebras

A1,1:X1=∂t,A1,2:X1=∂x,A1,3:X1=∂u.A_{1,1}:X_{1}=\partial_{t},\quad A_{1,2}:X_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad A_{1,3}:X_{1}=\partial_{u}. (5.1)

The corresponding invariant equations will have the form

A1,1\displaystyle A_{1,1} :ut=ux​x​x+F(x,u,ux,ux​x),\displaystyle:\quad u_{t}=u_{xxx}+F(x,u,u_{x},u_{xx}), (5.2a)
A1,2\displaystyle A_{1,2} :ut=ux​x​x+F(t,u,ux,ux​x),\displaystyle:\quad u_{t}=u_{xxx}+F(t,u,u_{x},u_{xx}), (5.2b)
A1,3\displaystyle A_{1,3} :ut=ux​x​x+F(x,t,ux,ux​x).\displaystyle:\quad u_{t}=u_{xxx}+F(x,t,u_{x},u_{xx}). (5.2c)
Theorem 5.1.

There are three inequivalent classes of equations (1.1) invariant under one-parameter symmetry group. Their representatives are given by (5.2).

5.2 Equations with two-dimensional symmetry algebras

There are two isomorphy classes of two-dimensional Lie algebras, abelian and non-abelian satisfying the commutation relations [X1,X2]=κ​X2[X_{1},X_{2}]=\kappa X_{2}, κ=0,1.\kappa=0,1. We denote them by A2,1A_{2,1} and A2,2A_{2,2}.

I. Abelian:

We start from each of the one-dimensional cases obtained in (5.1) and add to it vector fields X2X_{2} of the form (2.4) commuting with X1X_{1}. We then simplify X2X_{2} by equivalence transformations leaving the vector field X1X_{1} invariant. For further details we refer the reader to Ref. [4]. The standardized X2X_{2} and the restricted form of FF in (5.2) are then substituted into (2.5). Solving this equation will further restrict the form of the function FF. The number of variables of FF reduces by one, three variables in this case. Thus, we find that there exist precisely four classes of two-dimensional abelian symmetry algebras represented by the following ones:

Remark: Solvable nondecomposable algebras can be written as semidirect sums of a one-dimensional subalgebra {X3}\{X_{3}\} and an abelian ideal {X1,X2}\{X_{1},X_{2}\}. Note that the algebras A3,6A_{3,6} and A3,8A_{3,8} are isomorphic to 𝔢⁡(1,1)\mathfrak{e}(1,1), and 𝔢⁡(2)\mathfrak{e}(2), respectively. The algebra A3,3A_{3,3} is a nonabelian nilpotent algebra (Heisenberg algebra).

The commutation relations of the algebras in question can be represented in the matrix notation

([X1,X3][X2,X3])=J​(X1X2),[X1,X2]=0\left({\begin{array}[]{*{20}c}{[X_{1},X_{3}]}\\ {[X_{2},X_{3}]}\\ \end{array}}\right)=J\left({\begin{array}[]{*{20}c}{X_{1}}\\ {X_{2}}\\ \end{array}}\right),\quad[X_{1},X_{2}]=0

where JJ is a 2×22\times 2 real matrix that can be taken in Jordan canonical form.

A solvable three-dimensional Lie algebra always possesses a two-dimensional abelian ideal. We assume that the ideal {X1,X2}\{X_{1},X_{2}\} is already of the form (5.3) and add a third element X3X_{3} in the form (2.4) acting on the ideal. Imposing commutation relations and simplifying with equivalence transformations (2.6) (we consider each canonical form of the matrix individually) yield the realizations of solvable Lie algebras together with the corresponding invariant equations.

There exist nine classes of realizations of nilpotent algebras which give rise to invariant equations.

Theorem 5.3.

There are thirty-eight inequivalent three-dimensional solvable symmetry algebras admitted by equation (1.1).

6 Equations with four-dimensional solvable algebras

For dimL=4\dim L=4, we proceed exactly in the same manner as above. We start from the already standardized three-dimensional algebras, and add a further linearly independent element X4X_{4}, and require that they form a Lie algebra.

We preserve the notations of the previous section.

Nondecomposable algebras:

The set of inequivalent abstract four-dimensional Lie algebras contains ten real non-decomposable Lie algebras A4,i={X1A_{4,i}=\{X_{1}, X2,X3X_{2},X_{3}, X4}X_{4}\} (i=1,…,10)(i=1,\ldots,10) [4, 5]. They are all solvable and therefore can be written as semidirect sums of a one-dimensional Lie algebra {X4}\{X_{4}\} and a three-dimensional ideal N={X1,X2,X3}N=\{X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}\}. For A4,iA_{4,i} (i=1,…,6)(i=1,\ldots,6), NN is abelian, for A4,7,A4,8,A4,9A_{4,7},A_{4,8},A_{4,9} it is of type A3,3A_{3,3} (nilpotent), and for A4,10A_{4,10} it is of the type A3,5A_{3,5}. We sum up the above results as a theorem.

Theorem 6.1.

There exist fifty-two inequivalent four-dimensional symmetry algebras admitted by equation (1.1). The explicit forms of those algebras as well as the associated invariant equations are given above.

7 Discussion and Conclusions

This paper provides a symmetry classification of the KdV type equations involving an arbitrary function of five arguments. We find that the equivalence classes of invariant equations involve an arbitrary function of four, three, two variables and one variable as soon as the symmetry algebra is one-, two-, three-, and four-dimensional, respectively. In particular, we studied symmetries of the most general third-order linear evolution equation. What came out from this, to our surprise, is that the symmetry group allowed is four-dimensional at most, while there are nonlinear equations with symmetry algebras greater than four. This result is in contrast to the second-order evolution equations. It is exactly the linear heat equation that allows for the maximal symmetry algebra.

To complete the classification list, it only remains to obtain the inequivalent equations invariant under solvable algebras of the dimension dimL≥5\dim L\geq 5. But this would require to go through a large number of isomorphism classes. To give an idea of the complexity of this task let us recall that there are sixty-six classes of nonisomorphic real, solvable Lie algebras of dimension five. For dimension six, there exist ninety-nine classes of them with a nilpotent element. We plan to devote a separate article to study equations admitting higher-dimensional symmetry algebras.

Whenever FF is an arbitrary function of its arguments, the symmetry algebras given in the paper are maximal. In particular, if we impose the requirement that function FF is be independent of ux​xu_{xx} then we find that ϕ=R⁡(t)​u+S⁡(x,t)\phi=R(t)u+S(x,t) in (2.4). In this case, invariance under four-dimensional algebras will force FF to depend on an arbitrary constant rather than on an arbitrary function. Then, they may admit symmetry groups of the dimension higher than four. We have analyzed this restricted class of equations and obtained that the only equation whose symmetry algebra is higher than four is the one corresponding to the realization A4,11A_{4,1}^{1} for F~=const.\tilde{F}=\text{const.} On the other hand, for the specific choices of F~\tilde{F} involving one variable, the equations with four-dimensional symmetry algebras may be invariant under larger symmetry groups. For instance, the particular case of the equation invariant under A4,11A_{4,1}^{1} obtained by setting F~=c​ux​x4/3,\tilde{F}=cu_{xx}^{4/3}, c=const.c=\text{const.} admits an additional symmetry group generated by the dilation operator X5=3t∂t+x∂x−u∂uX_{5}=3t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x}-u\partial_{u}.

We only presented representative lists of equivalence classes of invariant equations. All other invariant equations can be recovered from these lists by applying the point transformations (2.6). In other words, an equation in the class (1.1) will have a symmetry group with dimension satisfying dimL≤6\dim L\leq 6 if and only if it can be transformed to one in the (canonical) equations from the list.

As we mentioned, our classification is performed within point transformations of coordinates. Two equations are equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by a change of variables. On the other hand, consider a special case of (6.2) for c=−3/4c=-3/4 [25]

ut=ux​x​x−34​ux​x2uxu_{t}=u_{xxx}-\frac{3}{4}\frac{u_{xx}^{2}}{u_{x}}

which additionally allows a symmetry group generated by {∂u}.\{\partial_{u}\}. Though this equation is equivalent to the third-order linear equation vt=vx​x​xv_{t}=v_{xxx} under the (no-point) transformation v=uxv=\sqrt{u_{x}}, we treat them as inequivalent.

To give a reader an insight into possible applications of the results of this article, we consider a subclass of equations (1.1)

ut=ux​x​x+u​ux+f⁡(t)​uu_{t}=u_{xxx}+uu_{x}+f(t)u (7.1)

which arises in several physical applications such as propagation of waves in shallow water of variable depth.

When f⁡(t)f(t) is arbitrary, (7.1) admits a two-dimensional abelian symmetry algebra generated by

X1=∂x,X2=ξ(t)∂x−ξ˙(t)∂u,ξ=∫exp{∫f(t)dt}dt.X_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad X_{2}=\xi(t)\partial_{x}-\dot{\xi}(t)\partial_{u},\quad\xi=\int\exp\{\int f(t)\;dt\}\;dt. (7.2)

By the change of dependent variable u~=u/ξ˙\tilde{u}=u/\dot{\xi}, the generators are transformed to the realization A2,13A_{2,1}^{3} with α=−ξ.\alpha=-\xi. The corresponding invariant equation takes the form

u~t=u~x​x​x+ξ˙​u~​u~x\tilde{u}_{t}=\tilde{u}_{xxx}+\dot{\xi}\tilde{u}\tilde{u}_{x}

which is a particular case of (1.2).

For the special case f⁡(t)=a​tk,(a≠0)f(t)=at^{k},\;(a\neq 0) the algebra is larger and we have the following possibilities for the algebra to be either three- or four-dimensional.

1.) (a,k)=(a,−1),(a,k)=(a,-1), a≠−1a\neq-1: The equation admits the three-dimensional indecomposable solvable symmetry algebra spanned by

X1=∂x,X2=t1+a∂x−(1+a)ta∂u,X3=t∂t+x3∂x−23u∂uX_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad X_{2}=t^{1+a}\partial_{x}-(1+a)t^{a}\partial_{u},\quad X_{3}=t\partial_{t}+\frac{x}{3}\partial_{x}-\frac{2}{3}u\partial_{u} (7.3)

with non-zero commutation relations

[X1,X3]=−13​X1,[X2,X3]=−3​a+23​X2.[X_{1},X_{3}]=-\frac{1}{3}X_{1},\quad[X_{2},X_{3}]=-\frac{3a+2}{3}X_{2}.

For a=−1/3a=-1/3, the algebra is isomorphic, up to scaling of basis elements, to A3,5A_{3,5}, for −1<a<−13-1<a<-\frac{1}{3}, to A3,7A_{3,7}.

For a=−2/3a=-2/3 it is isomorphic to the decomposable solvable algebra A3,2A_{3,2} and a suitable basis is

X1=∂x,X2=t1/3∂x−13t−2/3∂u,X3=t∂t+x3∂x−23u∂u.X_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad X_{2}=t^{1/3}\partial_{x}-\frac{1}{3}t^{-2/3}\partial_{u},\quad X_{3}=t\partial_{t}+\frac{x}{3}\partial_{x}-\frac{2}{3}u\partial_{u}.

With the equivalence transformation

t~=t,x~=x,u~=−3​t2/3​u,\tilde{t}=t,\quad\tilde{x}=x,\quad\tilde{u}=-3t^{2/3}u,

the basis elements are transformed, up to scaling, to the realization A3,23A_{3,2}^{3}. The transformed equation is

u~t=u~x​x​x−13t−2/3u~u~x.\tilde{u}_{t}=\tilde{u}_{xxx}-\frac{1}{3}t^{-2/3}\tilde{u}\tilde{u}_{x}.

This equation belongs to the class corresponding to the realization A3,23A_{3,2}^{3}.

We note that a member of (1.2) for f=1,f=1, g=t2g=t^{2} (see [1]) is equivalent, under appropriate point transformation, to the above equation. Similarly, the particular case a=−α/(1+α)a=-\alpha/(1+\alpha), α≠0,1,2\alpha\neq 0,1,2 is equivalent to f=1f=1, g=tαg=t^{\alpha} of (1.2). In this case, the symmetry algebra is indecomposable and solvable.

2.) (a,k)=(−1,−1)(a,k)=(-1,-1): the spherical KdV (sKdV) equation

In this case the equation is invariant with respect to a three-dimensional symmetry algebra. We choose its basis to be

X1=∂x,X2=lnt∂x−1t∂u,X3=t∂t+x3∂x−23u∂u,X_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad X_{2}=\ln t\partial_{x}-\frac{1}{t}\partial_{u},\quad X_{3}=t\partial_{t}+\frac{x}{3}\partial_{x}-\frac{2}{3}u\partial_{u}, (7.4)

with non-zero commutation relations

[X3,X1]=−13​X1,[X3,X2]=X1−13​X2.[X_{3},X_{1}]=-\frac{1}{3}X_{1},\quad[X_{3},X_{2}]=X_{1}-\frac{1}{3}X_{2}.

It is easy to see that this algebra is isomorphic to A3,4A_{3,4}. Under the transformation u~=3​t​u\tilde{u}=3tu, the generators are transformed to the realization A3,42A_{3,4}^{2}. The sKdV eq. takes the form

u~t=u~x​x​x+13​t​u~​u~x\tilde{u}_{t}=\tilde{u}_{xxx}+\frac{1}{3t}\tilde{u}\tilde{u}_{x}

which is a particular case of the equation invariant under the algebra A3,42A_{3,4}^{2}.

We note that a member of (1.2) for f=1,f=1, g=e3​tg=e^{3t} [1] is equivalent to the case 2.), i.e. the sKdV equation.

3.) (a,k)=(a,0)(a,k)=(a,0): The basis of the symmetry algebra reads as

X1=∂x,X2=ea​t(∂x−a∂u),X3=∂t,X_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad\quad X_{2}=e^{at}(\partial_{x}-a\partial_{u}),\quad X_{3}=\partial_{t}, (7.5)

with non-zero commutation relation [X3,X2]=a​X2[X_{3},X_{2}]=aX_{2}. The algebra is isomorphic to A3,2A_{3,2}. With the transformation u~=e−a​t​u\tilde{u}=e^{-at}u the equation is transformed to a special case of (1.2) for f=1,g=ea​t.f=1,g=e^{at}.

4.) (a,k)=(−1/2,−1)(a,k)=(-1/2,-1): the cylindrical KdV (cKdV) equation

In this case the symmetry algebra is four-dimensional. In a convenient basis we have

X1=2t∂x−1t∂u,X2=4t3/2∂t+2xt∂x−(xt+4tu)∂u,X3=∂x,X4=3t∂t+x∂x−2u∂u\begin{gathered}X_{1}=2\sqrt{t}\partial_{x}-\frac{1}{{\sqrt{t}}}\partial_{u},\hfill\\ X_{2}=4t^{3/2}\partial_{t}+2x\sqrt{t}\partial_{x}-(\frac{x}{{\sqrt{t}}}+4\sqrt{t}u)\partial_{u},\hfill\\ X_{3}=\partial_{x},\quad X_{4}=3t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x}-2u\partial_{u}\hfill\\ \end{gathered} (7.6)

with non-zero commutation relations

[X2,X3]=−X1,[X1,X4]=−12​X1,[X2,X4]=−32​X2,[X3,X4]=X3.[X_{2},X_{3}]=-X_{1},\quad[X_{1},X_{4}]=-\frac{1}{2}X_{1},\quad[X_{2},X_{4}]=-\frac{3}{2}X_{2},\quad[X_{3},X_{4}]=X_{3}.

We see that the symmetry algebra of cKdV equation is isomorphic to the algebra A4,8A_{4,8} with q=1q=1. The existence of such an isomorphism is a necessary, but not sufficient condition for a local point transforation to exist, transforming the two equations into each other. Comparing these generators with (2.10) and choosing (2.8) suitably, for example, first transforming the commuting elements {X1,X3}\{X_{1},X_{3}\} into {∂x~,t~∂x~+∂u~}\{\partial_{\tilde{x}},\tilde{t}\partial_{\tilde{x}}+\partial_{\tilde{u}}\} and then transforming the remaining ones with the aid of the freedom left in equivalence transformations we arrive at

t~=2t−1/2,x~=t−1/2x,u~=tu+x2\tilde{t}=2t^{-1/2},\quad\tilde{x}=t^{-1/2}x,\quad\tilde{u}=tu+\frac{x}{2}

which establishes the equivalence of the Lie algebra with basis (7.6) and cKdV equation to the KdV algebra (A4,81A_{4,8}^{1}) and KdV equation. This connection between the KdV and cKdV equations is well-known in the literature [19].

As a further comparison of the results obtained in the article we consider

ut+ux​x​x+f⁡(u)​uxk=0,k>0u_{t}+u_{xxx}+f(u)u_{x}^{k}=0,\quad k>0 (7.7)

which is clearly a special case of (1.1). Group classification of this equation is given in a table (see Table 2) [23]. These results can immediately be derived from those obtained in this paper either directly or performing a change of independent or dependent variables.

Note that the equations that do not appear in the classification list can be recovered from those by suitable point transformations.

A number of integrable KdV type equations can be reproduced by restricting the arbitrary functions contained in invariant equations of this article. For example, the realization A3,72A_{3,7}^{2} is equivalent to {∂t,∂x,t∂t+x/3∂x−u/3∂u}\{\partial_{t},\partial_{x},t\partial_{t}+x/3\partial_{x}-u/3\partial_{u}\} under the transformation u→u−1/3u\to u^{-1/3}. We have the invariant function

F=u4​F~​(ω1,ω2),ω1=u−2​ux,ω2=u−3​ux​x.F=u^{4}\tilde{F}(\omega_{1},\omega_{2}),\quad\omega_{1}=u^{-2}u_{x},\quad\omega_{2}=u^{-3}u_{xx}.

Setting F~=ω1\tilde{F}=\omega_{1} produces the modified KdV (mKdV) equation

ut=ux​x​x+u2​ux.u_{t}=u_{xxx}+u^{2}u_{x}. (7.8)

Since the maximal symmetry algebra of mKdV equation is three-dimensional, it is not isomorphic to the KdV algebra. This implies that there is no point transformation transforming the mKdV equation into KdV equation. In this respect let us mention that there is the well-known non-local transformation (Miura transformation)

u~=u2±6​i​ux\tilde{u}=u^{2}\pm\sqrt{6}iu_{x}

taking the mKdV (7.8) into the KdV equation u~t=u~x​x​x+u~​u~x\tilde{u}_{t}=\tilde{u}_{xxx}+\tilde{u}\tilde{u}_{x}. Another integrable equation which can be obtained from our classification is [24]

ut=ux​x​x+3​(ux​x​u2+3​u​ux2)+3​u4​ux.u_{t}=u_{xxx}+3(u_{xx}u^{2}+3uu_{x}^{2})+3u^{4}u_{x}.

Its symmetry algebra is isomorphic to A3,72A_{3,7}^{2}. We mention that this equation can be linearized by a change of dependent variable.

Let us mention also that a classification based on higher order symmetries of third-order integrable nonlinear equations of the form

ut=ux​x​x+F⁡(u,ux,ux​x)u_{t}=u_{xxx}+F(u,u_{x},u_{xx}) (7.9)

is given in [25].

Finally, let us point out that in a very recent work [26] a class of integrable (in the sense of existence of an infinite number of generalized symmetries) third-order evolution equations of the form (7.9) for specific FF admitting recursion operators have been analyzed. Among others, the special cases corresponding to F~=3​ω\tilde{F}=3\omega and F~=3/2−3​ω\tilde{F}=3/2-3\omega of (6.1) produce the following equations with 4-dimensional symmetry algebra A3,71⊕A1A_{3,7}^{1}\oplus A_{1}

ut=ux​x​x+3​u−1​ux​ux​x,ut=ux​x​x−3​u−1​ux​ux​x+32​u−2​ux3,\begin{gathered}u_{t}=u_{xxx}+3u^{-1}u_{x}u_{xx},\hfill\\ u_{t}=u_{xxx}-3u^{-1}u_{x}u_{xx}+\frac{3}{2}u^{-2}u_{x}^{3},\hfill\\ \end{gathered}

both of which were shown to admit recursion operators. This fact indicates that many equations with relatively large symmetry groups in our classification are among the most probable candidates for being integrable.

We note that the maximal symmetry algebra of the first equation of the above list is infinite-dimensional with basis elements

X1=∂t,X2=∂x,X3=t∂t+x3∂x+u2∂u,X_{1}=\partial_{t},\quad X_{2}=\partial_{x},\quad X_{3}=t\partial_{t}+\frac{x}{3}\partial_{x}+\frac{u}{2}\partial_{u},
X(ρ)=ρ(x,t)u−1∂u,ρt=ρx​x​x.X(\rho)=\rho(x,t)u^{-1}\partial_{u},\quad\rho_{t}=\rho_{xxx}.

The existence of an infinite-dimensional symmetry algebra suggests linearizability of the equation by point transformations and, indeed, it is linearized by the change of dependent variable v⁡(x,t)=u2​(x,t)/2v(x,t)=u^{2}(x,t)/2.
